title: Gravity lab
summary: Choose a mass and a planet, and see how hard gravity would pull on it.
intro: Everything with mass is pulled by gravity. Pick an example mass and a planet, guess what will happen, then work out the pull with a simple formula.
modelNote: This is a learning model, not a realistic physics simulation. It uses one measured gravity value for each planet.

input.label: Mass
input.hint: Type any mass from 0.1 to 1,000 kilograms, for example 10.

prediction.question: Before you look: will gravity pull on this mass less, about the same or more than on Earth?

options.text: About the same as on Earth

explanations: Mass is how much stuff something is made of. It is measured in kilograms (kg), and it stays the same on every planet.
Weight is a force: how hard gravity pulls on that mass. Forces are measured in newtons (N), so weight changes from planet to planet.
To work out the pull, multiply the mass by the planet's gravity: force = mass × gravity, or F = m × g.

title: Build a tiny solar system
summary: Shrink Earth to a bead and work out how big and how far away everything else would be.
intro: Choose how wide your model Earth is. Everything else is shrunk by the same amount, so you can see the true sizes and distances of the solar system.
modelNote: This is a learning model. The sizes and distances are calculated from real measurements, all shrunk by the same amount.

input.label: Model Earth's diameter
input.hint: Type any width from 0.5 to 5 centimetres, with up to 2 decimal places, or use the slider. The slider and the number always match.

prediction.question: Optional guess: with Earth this size, how far from the Sun would Neptune be?

diameterNote: Diameters used: NASA's equatorial diameters for the planets, measured across the middle. For the Sun, twice NASA's volumetric mean radius: the width of a perfect ball with the same volume.
distanceNote: Distances are averages. Each planet's path around the Sun is not a perfect circle, so its real distance changes as it moves, and the planets are almost never lined up in a row like this table.
pictureNote: There is no picture here on purpose: a drawing that showed these sizes and distances to the same scale would be far too big for the screen.
